title: Counting a Nation
sub: Grades 5–8 · Math · Data and proportion from 1776 to 50 stars

hero.credit: Emanuel Leutze, *Washington Crossing the Delaware*, 1851. The Metropolitan Museum of Art. Public domain.

objective: Students will turn the exhibition’s record of the flag, a new star for each state in the year it joined the Union, into a **frequency table and bar graph by decade**, and describe what the graph shows and hides. Then they will use **percents and ratios** with the numbers the posters give for 1776, and ask what an approximate number such as *perhaps 3,000* can and cannot tell us.

objectives.heading: By the end of this lesson you will be able to:
objectives.why: The story of a nation is also a story told in numbers. Reading them carefully, and knowing when a number is only an estimate, is how we keep from being fooled by them.

materials: *Add a Star*, projected; *A Copy of a Copy* and the poster *We Shall All Hang Together*
The *Show your class* page (page 3); calculators; differentiated handouts, one per student
connection: **Visit the exhibition:** play *Add a Star* to the end, and compare the class score with the bar graph. On the poster *We Shall All Hang Together*, find each number of the army in its chapter, *The War That Nearly Was Not Won*.

steps.title: Guess the decade
script: Open *Add a Star*. *“The flag began with 13 stars. Now it has 50. In which decade do you think the most states joined?”* Students write a guess. Play the first three jumps as a class, voting on the decade before each new star goes on. A bullseye scores 3 points; one decade out scores 1. *“Today we stop guessing and let the data answer.”*

screen.question: The flag began with 13 stars. Now it has 50. In which decade do you think the most states joined?

steps.purpose: Make a prediction the data can test.
students: Play three jumps of Add a Star: a bullseye scores 3, one decade out scores 1.

steps.title: The stars by decade
script: The flag began with 13 stars for the 13 states that had been the Thirteen Colonies. Thirty-seven more states joined. Show the table on page 3: each state’s star, grouped by the decade it joined. Model one row as a tally and one bar on a graph.

Read the data together. The **mode** is the 1810s, with five states. Three decades, the 1920s, 1930s and 1940s, have **none**. The **range** of years runs from 1791 to 1959, which is 168 years, and the **longest gap** is from 1912 to 1959, 47 years. Ask: *what does a bar graph by decade hide?* Two states in 1959 look the same as two states ten years apart.

steps.purpose: Organize the flag’s growth into a frequency table, then read it.

steps.title: The numbers of 1776
script: Now the numbers on the poster *We Shall All Hang Together*: Washington’s army of approximately 19,000 against 32,000 British troops on Staten Island; by November, perhaps 3,000 effective troops. Work the ratio and the percent decrease, then the copies: about 200 Dunlap broadsides, 26 known to survive. Stress the words *approximately*, *perhaps* and *about*: an answer cannot be more exact than the numbers it starts from.

examples.title: Two armies
examples.answer: About 1.7 British troops for every American soldier

steps.purpose: Use ratio and percent to see the odds the signers faced, and how few first printings survive.
students: Why does the poster say *approximately* and *perhaps*?

steps.title: Choose a handout
script: Students choose a handout. All three levels use the same stars and the same numbers from 1776.

levels.name: Green Level
levels.summary: Count the states in each decade and draw a bar graph. Find the decade with the most and the decades with none, and work out how many years passed between pairs of dates.

levels.name: Yellow Level
levels.summary: Build the frequency table and bar graph, find the mode, range and longest gap, then work out a ratio and two percents from the numbers of 1776.

levels.name: Red Level
levels.summary: Compare the first and second halves of the data, find percents and rates, and judge what *approximately* and *perhaps* do to an answer, and what a graph by decade hides.

steps.purpose: Practice with the same data at the right level of challenge.
students: Choose Green, Yellow or Red. All three use the same stars and the same numbers from 1776.

steps.title: Back to the guess
script: Return to the guesses from the hook. Who chose the 1810s? Ask one student from each level to share one finding. Then ask: *what can these numbers not tell us?* The data shows when states joined; it says nothing about how or why.

screen.question: The flag began with 13 stars. Now it has 50. In which decade do you think the most states joined?

steps.purpose: Test the hook’s guesses against the data, and name one thing the numbers cannot say.
students: Name one thing these numbers cannot tell us.

steps.title: Look back
script: Put the objectives back on the screen, asked as questions: *“Can you now…?”* For each one, students show a thumb up, sideways or down. Ask one student to answer each aloud; for the last, ask a Red Level reader.
